K-Nearest Neighbor Imputation for Numeric Matrices

Source: R/knn_imp.R
knn_imp.Rd

Impute missing values in a numeric matrix with K-nearest neighbors (K-NN), searching the whole matrix for neighbors.

Usage

knn_imp(
  obj,
  k,
  colmax = 0.9,
  method = c("euclidean", "manhattan"),
  cores = 1,
  post_imp = TRUE,
  subset = NULL,
  dist_pow = 0,
  .progress = FALSE
)

Arguments

obj

A double matrix. Samples are in rows and features in columns.

k

Integer. Number of nearest neighbors for K-NN imputation.

colmax

Numeric scalar between 0 and 1. Columns with a proportion of missing values greater than colmax take no part in the imputation, as described under Column mean fill.

method

Character. One of "euclidean" or "manhattan". The distance used to find neighbors, as defined under Details.

cores

Integer. Number of cores for K-NN imputation. Defaults to 1.

post_imp

Logical. If TRUE, column means replace the missing values that remain after imputation, as described under Column mean fill.

subset

Optional character or integer vector. The columns to impute and return, by name or by number, or NULL for every column. Defaults to NULL.

dist_pow

Numeric. Power used to penalize more distant neighbors in the weighted average, where 0 gives an unweighted average. The weighting rule is given under Details in knn_imp().

.progress

Logical. If TRUE, show imputation progress.

Value

A slideimp_results object: a numeric matrix with the rows of obj and the columns that subset selects, with missing values imputed.

Details

knn_imp() imputes each column from the k columns nearest to it, found by an exact brute-force search. The distance between the target column and a candidate column is a mean over the rows where both are observed. Candidates that share different numbers of rows with the target therefore stay comparable. method = "euclidean" averages squared differences and takes no square root. method = "manhattan" averages absolute differences.

A candidate that shares no observed row with the target is never a neighbor. A column can therefore have fewer than k neighbors, or none, and K-NN does not impute a column with none.

A column with few observed values can be selected as a neighbor because it agrees with the target on one or two shared rows. Such a neighbor has no value at most of the rows to impute. A lower colmax keeps these columns out of the neighbors.

When dist_pow > 0, imputed values are distance-weighted averages of the selected neighbors: a neighbor at distance d is weighted (d_min / d)^dist_pow, where d_min is the smallest positive distance among the neighbors chosen for that column. d_min cancels out of the average and only keeps the largest weight at 1.

Under "euclidean", d is a mean squared difference, so weighting by 1 / d^dist_pow equals weighting by 1 / d^(2 * dist_pow) on the usual, square-rooted euclidean distance. A dist_pow tuned for one method therefore does not carry over to the other.

Neighbors are selected once per column. A neighbor that is missing at a row drops out of the average for that row, which is taken over the neighbors observed there. K-NN does not impute a row where none of the neighbors is observed.

With dist_pow > 0, a neighbor at distance zero agrees with the target on every shared row and would take an infinite weight. It takes weight 1 instead, and the other neighbors take a small positive weight. Exact matches therefore dominate the average, but the other neighbors stay in it. When every neighbor is at distance zero, all weights are 1.

The result holds the subset columns in the order they have in obj. Every column within colmax can still be a neighbor, in subset or not. A name that is not in colnames(obj), or a subset that selects no column, is an error.

K-NN performance optimization

  • Use subset when only specific columns need imputation.

  • Use group_imp() or slide_imp() for very large matrices.

Column mean fill

A column with a proportion of missing values greater than colmax takes no part in the imputation. The method neither uses the column to impute other columns nor imputes it.

With post_imp = TRUE, column means replace the missing values that remain after the method has run. Two kinds of missing value can remain: the missing values of the columns that took no part, and the cells for which the method found no value. Each column mean is the mean of the column's observed values. With post_imp = FALSE, both kinds stay missing.

The result records what the column means replaced, in two attributes:

  • mean_filled_cols: an integer vector with the index, in the result, of each column that took no part and was filled.

  • mean_filled_cells: an integer matrix with the columns row and col, one row for each cell that the method could not impute and that was filled.

Both attributes are empty when no column mean was used. print() reports them when they are not empty.

Missing values and non-finite input

obj must be a double matrix. An integer or logical matrix is rejected, not converted. Convert one with storage.mode(obj) <- "double".

NA and NaN are both treated as missing. The package does not distinguish between them.

Inf and -Inf are rejected on entry, and so is a column with no observed values (every cell NA or NaN). Locate them with which(is.infinite(obj), arr.ind = TRUE) and which(colSums(!is.na(obj)) == 0).

References

Troyanskaya O, Cantor M, Sherlock G, Brown P, Hastie T, Tibshirani R, Botstein D, Altman RB (2001). Missing value estimation methods for DNA microarrays. Bioinformatics, 17(6), 520-525. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/17.6.520

See also

group_imp() to impute within feature groups.

Examples

set.seed(123)
obj <- sim_mat(20, 20, perc_col_na = 1)$input
sum(is.na(obj))
#> [1] 40

# Select `k` with `tune_imp()`.
result <- knn_imp(obj, k = 10)
result
#> Method: K-NN imputation
#> Dimensions: 20 x 20
#> 
#>           feature1  feature2  feature3  feature4  feature5  feature6
#> sample1 0.08885928 0.0946424 0.5010982 0.2257198 0.3310293 0.3919172
#> sample2 0.35087647 0.2569208 0.4441198 0.3953534 0.5894579 0.2589739
#> sample3 0.56864697 0.4021824 0.7354948 0.6422099 0.8454413 0.6652821
#> sample4 0.30420093 0.7886995 0.3732225 0.5291319 0.5289648 0.4384578
#> sample5 0.34030847 0.6095144 0.3741498 0.3364915 0.4772101 0.8290134
#> sample6 0.45667473 0.4614949 0.8676809 0.7274044 0.9167450 0.6643710
#> # Showing 6 of 20 rows and 6 of 20 columns

# Impute and return only the first three columns
knn_imp(obj, k = 10, subset = 1:3)
#> Method: K-NN imputation
#> Dimensions: 20 x 3
#> 
#>           feature1  feature2  feature3
#> sample1 0.08885928 0.0946424 0.5010982
#> sample2 0.35087647 0.2569208 0.4441198
#> sample3 0.56864697 0.4021824 0.7354948
#> sample4 0.30420093 0.7886995 0.3732225
#> sample5 0.34030847 0.6095144 0.3741498
#> sample6 0.45667473 0.4614949 0.8676809
#> # Showing 6 of 20 rows and 3 of 3 columns
